description: The algebraic identity (z₁-z₃)(z₂-z₄) = (z₁-z₂)(z₃-z₄) + (z₂-z₃)(z₁-z₄) yields Ptolemy's inequality via the triangle inequality in ℂ

overview.historicalContext: The complex-number proof of Ptolemy's theorem is perhaps the most elegant approach to this classical result. While Ptolemy himself used a geometric argument in the *Almagest* (c. 150 AD), the complex-number proof reveals the deeper algebraic structure: the identity $(z_1 - z_3)(z_2 - z_4) = (z_1 - z_2)(z_3 - z_4) + (z_2 - z_3)(z_1 - z_4)$ holds in any commutative ring, and Ptolemy's inequality follows from taking absolute values in $\mathbb{C}$.
overview.problemStatement:
**Ptolemy's Inequality (Complex Number Proof)**:

For any four points $z_1, z_2, z_3, z_4 \in \mathbb{C}$:

$$|z_1 - z_3| \cdot |z_2 - z_4| \leq |z_1 - z_2| \cdot |z_3 - z_4| + |z_2 - z_3| \cdot |z_1 - z_4|$$

with equality if and only if the four points are concyclic.
overview.text: The algebraic identity (z₁-z₃)(z₂-z₄) = (z₁-z₂)(z₃-z₄) + (z₂-z₃)(z₁-z₄) combined with the triangle inequality gives Ptolemy's inequality over ℂ
overview.proofStrategy:
The proof has two components:
1. **Algebraic identity**: $(z_1-z_3)(z_2-z_4) = (z_1-z_2)(z_3-z_4) + (z_2-z_3)(z_1-z_4)$ holds in any commutative ring, proved by `ring`.
2. **Ptolemy's inequality**: Taking norms of both sides, the LHS becomes $\|z_1-z_3\| \cdot \|z_2-z_4\|$ by multiplicativity of norm (`norm_mul`). The RHS is bounded above by $\|z_1-z_2\| \cdot \|z_3-z_4\| + \|z_2-z_3\| \cdot \|z_1-z_4\|$ via the triangle inequality (`norm_add_le`) and multiplicativity.
keyInsights: The identity (z₁-z₃)(z₂-z₄) = (z₁-z₂)(z₃-z₄) + (z₂-z₃)(z₁-z₄) holds over any commutative ring, not just ℂ. Ptolemy is fundamentally algebraic, with the geometry entering only through the norm.
The entire proof of Ptolemy's inequality is three steps: multiplicativity of norm, the algebraic identity, and the triangle inequality. This is arguably the shortest known proof.

This approach yields the inequality form (≤) rather than equality. Equality requires the additional geometric condition that the four points are concyclic, which corresponds to the equality case of the triangle inequality.

The proof reveals a contrast with the geometric approach: the Mathlib cospherical formulation proves equality directly for concyclic points, while the complex-number proof naturally gives the inequality for all four-point configurations.

sections.title: Module Header and Imports
sections.summary: Documentation and imports. Uses Mathlib.Analysis.Complex.Basic for ℂ and its normed field structure, Topology.MetricSpace.Basic for dist, and Tactic for proof automation.
sections.mathContext: The imports provide ℂ as a normed field (giving norm_mul and norm_add_le) and as a metric space (giving dist_eq_norm).

sections.title: The Algebraic Identity
sections.summary: The identity (z₁-z₃)(z₂-z₄) = (z₁-z₂)(z₃-z₄) + (z₂-z₃)(z₁-z₄) proved over any CommRing by ring, then specialized to ℂ.
sections.mathContext: This identity is the algebraic core of Ptolemy's theorem. It expresses the 'diagonal product' as a sum of two 'opposite side products'. The ring tactic verifies this by expansion.

sections.title: Ptolemy's Inequality (Norm Form)
sections.summary: Ptolemy's inequality ‖z₁-z₃‖·‖z₂-z₄‖ ≤ ‖z₁-z₂‖·‖z₃-z₄‖ + ‖z₂-z₃‖·‖z₁-z₄‖ via a calc proof using norm_mul and norm_add_le.
sections.mathContext: The calc proof chains: (1) norm_mul rewrites ‖a‖·‖b‖ as ‖a·b‖, (2) the algebraic identity rewrites the product as a sum, (3) norm_add_le gives the triangle inequality, (4) norm_mul expands back.

sections.title: Alternative Formulations
sections.summary: Two equivalent formulations: using Complex.abs (via Complex.norm_eq_abs) and using dist (via dist_eq_norm).
sections.mathContext: Complex.abs and ‖·‖ agree on ℂ. The dist formulation dist(z₁,z₃)·dist(z₂,z₄) ≤ dist(z₁,z₂)·dist(z₃,z₄) + dist(z₂,z₃)·dist(z₁,z₄) connects directly to the classical geometric statement.

sections.title: Equality Characterization
sections.summary: Sufficient condition for Ptolemy's equality: if (z₂-z₃)(z₁-z₄) = t·(z₁-z₂)(z₃-z₄) for some real t ≥ 0, both sides equal (1+t)·‖(z₁-z₂)(z₃-z₄)‖.
sections.mathContext: The equality case of the triangle inequality ‖a+b‖ ≤ ‖a‖+‖b‖ occurs when a and b point in the same direction. For Ptolemy, this means the two opposite-side products are positively proportional. Geometrically, concyclic points in the standard ordering satisfy this condition.

sections.title: Numerical Examples
sections.summary: Numerical verification for the unit square vertices 0, 1, 1+i, i where equality holds (2 = 1·1 + 1·1).
sections.mathContext: The four vertices of the unit square lie on a circle of radius √2/2, so Ptolemy's equality holds. The diagonal products equal 2, matching the sum of opposite side products.

crossReferences.description: PtolemysTheorem.lean proves equality for cospherical points using Mathlib's geometric approach. This file proves the inequality for arbitrary points using the algebraic/complex-number approach.

conclusion.summary: A complete complex-number proof of Ptolemy's inequality with equality characterization. Starting from a purely algebraic identity over any commutative ring, the inequality follows from multiplicativity of norm and the triangle inequality. The equality condition (when opposite-side products are positively proportional) is also proved. Six theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications:
**Theoretical Significance**: The complex-number proof reveals the algebraic essence of Ptolemy's theorem. While the geometric proof works with cospherical points and angle conditions, the algebraic proof needs only a commutative ring and a norm satisfying the triangle inequality. This explains why Ptolemy-type results appear in many settings beyond Euclidean geometry.

The inequality form is strictly more general than the equality: it holds for all four-point configurations in ℂ, with the geometric condition (concyclicity) characterizing when equality holds.
openQuestions: Can the converse direction be proved: if Ptolemy's equality holds, are the opposite-side products necessarily positively proportional (equivalently, are the points concyclic)?
Can the derivation of the sine addition formula from Ptolemy's theorem be formalized, showing the historical connection between chord tables and modern trigonometry?
